source_title: Bob Costas on Susan Saint James’ ‘Inspirational’ Strength After Son’s Death (Exclusive) - People.com
source_excerpt:
The close friends of the actress, who died on Oct. 26 at age 80, open up about how she handled her heartbreak with incredible grace
Bob Costas, Tom Werner and Sandy Montag share personal memories of Susan Saint James following the actress’ death at age 80
The actress lost her youngest son, Teddy, 14, in a 2004 plane crash that also seriously injured her husband, Dick Ebersol, and their older son Charlie
Costas recalls Saint James’ “magnificent” eulogy for Teddy, while Werner remembers how she turned her grief into a “celebration of life”
Susan Saint James ’ longtime friends are remembering the remarkable strength she showed following the devastating loss of her youngest son, Teddy, and how she continued to celebrate his life even in her grief.
The actress, who died on Oct. 26 at age 80, lost Teddy, 14, in a private plane crash in Colorado over Thanksgiving weekend in 2004. Her husband, former NBC Sports chairman Dick Ebersol , and their older son Charlie, then 21, survived with serious injuries.
“It was inspirational,” television producer and longtime family friend Tom Werner tells PEOPLE of how Saint James handled the tragedy with grace and strength.
“She always thought about this terrible tragedy and turned it into a celebration of life,” recalls Werner, chairman of the Boston Red Sox.
“Whenever Dick and Susan came to Fenway Park, Susan would always talk about him in this mode of, ‘I am so grateful for the time that I spent with Teddy.’ She handled this terrible tragedy in such a life-affirming way.”

“She also loved to talk about what a big Red Sox fan he was,” he continues. “She just thought that the gift that he gave to that family, even though it was a short, short life, was something to be celebrated. So she did that.”
Sportscaster Bob Costas, who became close with Saint James through his longtime friendship with Ebersol, was equally moved by the eulogy she delivered at Teddy’s funeral.
“The eulogy she delivered for him under that kind of duress was just magnificent,” Costas tells PEOPLE, adding, “You wouldn’t think that something that heartbreaking could also be so beautiful.”
For family friend Sandy Montag, Saint James’ ability to support those around her while continuing to honor Teddy’s life was especially moving.
“The way she carried herself, and the way she was a rock for her family, and how she kept Teddy’s memory alive — and by the way, the whole family still does that — is something that is so inspirational,” Montag says.
“With everything that she went through in her life, she was always, always an uplifting person,” Montag adds. “She was devoted to everything that she did. She didn’t do anything halfway. She was all in.”
Beyond her resilience, Saint James’ friends remember her as someone who made everyone she encountered feel special.
“She was a big star in the ‘60s, ‘70s and ‘80s, but she never big-timed anybody,” Costas says.
“The minute you met her, she was warm and friendly and appreciative and either knew something about you or, more importantly, wanted to know about you.”
He adds, “There was a little bit, in the best sense of the word, some of that ‘60s and ‘70s flower child in her still. The kindness, the empathy, the openheartedness, the appreciation of others. In some sense, you outgrow that as you get older, but not Susan. The heart of it remained.”
Montag similarly remembers Saint James’ genuine interest in others and her ability to make those around her feel at ease.
“She loved to talk. She loved relationships of all kinds. She loved communicating. She loved to laugh. She was inquisitive. Just spending time with her was always a warm feeling,” he recalls. “She made you feel warm.”
For Montag, who lost his mother more than two decades ago, Saint James’ kindness offered a particularly personal source of comfort.
“I lost my mother 24 years ago. And when I would talk to Susan, I felt like I had a mom again.”
